domains.summary: Computer science theory for practitioners: computability, complexity, and logic, taught through consequences not proofs. General educational material; confers no certificate and implies no endorsement.

scenarios.title: Which algorithm wins
scenarios.situation: Two sorting implementations: A does roughly n^2 operations, B does roughly n log n. On 100 elements, A finishes first in your benchmark. Your dataset will grow to 10 million elements.
choices: B, because asymptotic growth dominates: constants decide small inputs, but n log n versus n^2 decides 10 million
A, because the benchmark proves it is faster
A, but rewrite it in a faster language
Neither; buy a bigger machine and keep A
scenarios.why: Big-O describes how cost scales, and scaling is what kills you: at n=10^7, n^2 is 10^14 operations versus ~2.4x10^8 for n log n, a gap no constant factor or hardware upgrade closes. Benchmarks on tiny inputs measure constants; Big-O predicts the future.
scenarios.hint: What does each algorithm cost when n grows by a factor of 100,000?

scenarios.title: Parsing HTML with regex
scenarios.situation:
A teammate proposes validating nested HTML tags with a single regular expression. It works on the test cases: bold and

x

.
choices: Regular expressions describe regular languages, which cannot count arbitrarily deep nesting; nested tags need at least a context-free grammar (a real parser)
There is no problem; the tests pass so it works
Regex is too slow for HTML; that is the only issue
HTML is not a real language so theory does not apply
scenarios.why: This is the Chomsky hierarchy in practice: finite automata (regex) have no stack, so they cannot match arbitrarily nested structures. It works on shallow test cases and fails on the deep or malformed real-world cases. Nested markup is the canonical example of a context-free (not regular) language: use a parser.
scenarios.hint: What machinery would you need to remember how many tags are still open?

scenarios.title: The perfect bug finder
scenarios.situation: A startup pitches you: 'Our AI analyzes any program and guarantees to tell you whether it will ever crash or loop forever.' They want you to integrate it into your CI pipeline as a hard gate.
choices: It is impossible in general: the halting problem is undecidable, so no tool can correctly decide termination for all programs
It is possible with enough compute; theory is just pessimism
It is possible for Python but not for C
It works as long as the AI was trained on enough code
scenarios.why: Turing proved no algorithm decides halting for all programs: any claimed decider can be fed a program that does the opposite of its verdict, a contradiction. Practical tools approximate (timeouts, heuristics, restricted language subsets), but 'guaranteed for any program' contradicts a proven impossibility. The language does not matter.
scenarios.hint: What happens if you feed their analyzer a program that loops exactly when the analyzer says 'halts'?

scenarios.title: The impossible schedule
scenarios.situation: Operations wants an optimizer that finds the provably optimal delivery schedule across 500 stops with time windows. They note 'computers are fast now' and ask why the prototype takes hours.
scenarios.prompt: How do you explain the difficulty?
choices: Optimal routing with constraints is NP-hard: no known algorithm scales polynomially, so you should target good approximations or heuristics, not provable optima
The prototype is just badly coded; a rewrite in a faster language will fix it
NP-hard means unsolvable; tell them it can never be done
Buy a quantum computer, which solves NP-hard problems instantly
scenarios.why: NP-hardness is a statement about scaling, not effort: the search space grows exponentially, so doubling the hardware barely moves the solvable size. The professional response is to change the goal: approximation algorithms, heuristics, and constraint solvers find excellent (not provably optimal) schedules fast. NP-hard does not mean impossible, and quantum computers are not magic oracles for it.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the search space when you add the 501st stop?

scenarios.title: Which way does the reduction go
scenarios.situation: You want to argue that your new problem X is computationally hard. You know problem Y (timetabling) is NP-complete. A colleague suggests 'reducing X to Y' to prove X is hard.
choices: No: to prove X is hard you reduce the known-hard Y to X, showing X is at least as hard as Y; reducing X to Y would show X is no harder than Y
Yes: reducing X to the known problem Y proves X inherits Y's hardness
Direction does not matter; any reduction between them proves both are hard
Reductions only apply to decidability, not complexity
scenarios.why: Reductions transfer hardness from the known problem to the new one: a reduction from Y to X means 'if I could solve X, I could solve Y,' so X is at least as hard as Y. The reverse direction shows X is at most as hard as Y (an upper bound, useful for algorithms, useless for hardness proofs). Getting the arrow backwards is the classic error.
scenarios.hint: If solving X gave you Y for free, which one is the harder problem?

scenarios.title: Decide this property
scenarios.situation: A manager asks for a tool that, given any program, decides whether it 'contains no security vulnerabilities.' The team debates whether this is merely difficult or fundamentally impossible.
scenarios.prompt: What does theory say, and what is the practical consequence?
choices: Rice's theorem: any non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable, so perfect detection is impossible; invest in layered approximations (linters, tests, review, fuzzing) instead of chasing certainty
It is merely difficult; more engineers will eventually solve it
It is decidable but NP-complete, so it needs more compute
It is possible if you restrict to memory-safe languages
scenarios.why: Rice's theorem generalizes the halting result: no algorithm decides any non-trivial property of what a program does (as opposed to its syntax). 'Has no vulnerabilities' is semantic, so perfection is ruled out in every language. The practical consequence is defense in depth with imperfect tools, each catching a different slice, rather than one guaranteed gate.
scenarios.hint: Is 'vulnerability-free' a property of the code text or of what the code does?

lessons.title: Theory — Core concepts
concepts: Big-O is about scaling, not speed: it tells you what happens when n grows 1000x, which is the question that decides architectures.
The Chomsky hierarchy matches machinery to languages: finite automata (regex) cannot count nesting; pushdown automata (parsers) can; know which tool your problem needs.
The halting problem is undecidable: no program decides termination for all programs, so every analyzer is an approximation with blind spots.
P versus NP is about verification versus discovery: NP problems have efficiently checkable solutions; NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP, and hardness transfers via reductions.
Reductions have a direction: reduce known-hard Y to new X to prove X hard ('X solves Y'); the reverse proves an upper bound, not hardness.
Rice's theorem kills perfect tools: no algorithm decides any non-trivial semantic property of programs, so security and correctness rest on layered imperfect methods.

example.walkthrough: A regular expression is a finite automaton: perfect for fixed-shape patterns like phone numbers, no memory of depth. The moment your pattern needs to count open versus close tags, you have left regular languages and need a parser.

pitfalls: Common trap: 'NP' means 'non-polynomial'; it means nondeterministic polynomial (efficiently verifiable).
Common trap: treating Big-O as exact timing; it drops constants and lower terms by design.
Common trap: reducing in the wrong direction and 'proving' hardness backwards.
Common trap: assuming a hard problem is unsolvable; NP-hard invites approximation, not surrender.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Classify the problem
labs.objective: Given six problem descriptions, classify each by decidability and complexity class.
steps: Read problems.txt: six short problem descriptions.
For each, decide: decidable or undecidable, with one-sentence justification.
For the decidable ones, label P, NP, or NP-hard/NP-complete as appropriate.
Note which practical approach fits each: exact algorithm, approximation, or heuristic.

checks.hint: At least one problem should be classified undecidable with justification.
Confirm all six problems are classified.

labs.title: Sketch a reduction
labs.objective: Write a reduction sketch proving a scheduling problem NP-hard, in the correct direction.
steps: Pick a known NP-complete problem (e.g., 3-SAT or vertex cover) as your source.
Define the mapping from source instances to scheduling instances.
Argue the mapping is polynomial-time computable.
Argue yes-instances map to yes-instances and back.
Write the sketch to reduction.txt with the direction stated explicitly.

checks.hint: State the reduction direction explicitly: known-hard problem reduces to your problem.

simulations.title: P vs NP in the standup
simulations.brief: The routing team needs optimal delivery routes for 200 stops by Friday. Someone suggests 'just try all permutations.' You know why that fails. Decide what ships.

steps.symptom: 200 stops, optimal routes, Friday deadline. Proposal: brute-force all permutations and pick the best.
evidence:
Stops: 200 | approach: enumerate all permutations
Deadline: Friday | claim: 'computers are fast now'
options: Approve — modern hardware can handle it
Reject with the math: 200! is ~10^374 permutations — more than atoms in the universe times itself. Brute force is not slow, it is impossible
Rent a bigger cluster for the enumeration
Reduce to 10 stops so brute force works
steps.explain: Factorial growth is not a performance problem — it is a physics problem. 200! dwarfs the age of the universe in nanoseconds. Complexity theory is not academic here; it is the difference between a plan and a fantasy.

steps.symptom: Brute force is dead. The team asks what actually ships Friday.
evidence: Need: good routes by Friday | optimal: provably impossible at this scale
options: Ship nothing — the problem is unsolvable
Ship a heuristic: nearest-neighbor plus local improvement gets within a few percent of optimal in seconds — and say so honestly
Wait for a quantum computer
Hire more drivers instead of optimizing
steps.explain: NP-hard means 'no known efficient exact algorithm' — not 'give up.' Heuristics and approximation algorithms exist precisely for this: near-optimal answers at industrial speed, with the approximation gap stated honestly. Theory tells you what not to attempt; engineering tells you what ships.

steps.symptom: Heuristic shipped: routes 4% longer than the theoretical optimum, computed in 11 seconds. How do you present it?
evidence:
Routes: within 4% of optimal | compute: 11s
Stakeholder question: 'Why not optimal?'
options: 'The algorithm is optimal.'
'Optimal would take longer than the universe; we get within 4% in 11 seconds. That 4% costs us roughly $X/week — here is the trade, in dollars.'
'Nobody needs optimal.'
Hide the 4% gap
steps.explain: Approximation is a business decision once you price the gap: 4% longer routes = $X/week, versus the impossibility of optimal. Theory gave you the impossibility proof; arithmetic gives you the price tag. Present both.

simulations.debrief: You killed the fantasy with factorial math, shipped the heuristic honestly, and priced the approximation gap. Complexity theory is project management for the impossible.

simulations.title: The halting helpdesk ticket
simulations.brief: Ticket: 'Write a linter rule that detects ALL infinite loops before deployment.' The requester is serious, senior, and wrong in an interesting way. Handle it.

steps.symptom: The ticket asks for a perfect infinite-loop detector. The requester cites 'AI advances' as evidence it is now possible.
evidence:
'Detect all infinite loops pre-deploy'
Requester: senior eng | justification: 'AI can do anything now'
options: Assign it to the team as a stretch goal
Explain the halting problem: no program can correctly decide halting for ALL programs — it is proven impossible, not merely hard. Then offer what IS possible
Buy an AI tool that claims to do it
Close the ticket as 'won't fix' with no explanation
steps.explain: The halting problem is undecidable — proven, not conjectured. No amount of AI changes a mathematical impossibility; a tool that 'detects all infinite loops' is either unsound or incomplete by necessity. 'Won't fix' without the explanation wastes the teaching moment.

steps.symptom: The requester accepts the proof but asks: 'So we just deploy infinite loops and hope?'
evidence: 'What DO we do about runaway processes?'
options: 'Yes, hope is the strategy.'

Offer the decidable substitutes: timeouts, resource limits, loop-complexity heuristics, and termination proofs for the specific patterns you actually use — impossibility of the general case does not block the practical cases
Write the perfect detector anyway
Ban loops in the codebase
steps.explain: Undecidable in general, manageable in practice: timeouts bound the damage, resource limits contain it, and heuristics catch the common patterns. Theory draws the boundary of the possible; engineering works the territory inside it.

steps.symptom: Timeouts and limits are in. A junior asks why the linter still misses some infinite loops.
options: 'We did — the linter is just buggy.'
'We bounded the damage, we did not solve the problem — and we cannot, provably. Knowing which problems are impossible is what keeps us from wasting sprints on them.'
'Don't worry about it.'
Assign the junior to fix the linter
steps.explain: The deepest lesson: knowing a problem is impossible is productive knowledge — it redirects effort from the unwinnable to the winnable. That is what computability theory is for: a map of where not to dig.

simulations.debrief: You delivered the impossibility proof with kindness, offered the practical substitutes, and taught the team to read the map. Undecidability is not despair — it is direction.

simulations.title: Exponential blowup
simulations.brief: The recursive Fibonacci service handles n=30 fine and dies at n=50. The code 'works' — it just never finishes. Find the complexity bug.

steps.symptom: fib(30) returns in a second. fib(50) has been running for an hour. Same code, same machine.
options: Add more CPU — n=50 just needs power
Recognize the exponential: naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems ~2^n times — n=50 needs ~10^10 calls. Memoize or go iterative
Rewrite it in a faster language
Cache the results in a database
steps.explain: Each call doubles the work: O(2^n). n=30 is a billion-ish operations (fine); n=50 is a quadrillion (not fine). The bug is not in the logic — it is in the complexity class. Memoization drops it to O(n) because each subproblem gets solved once.

steps.symptom: Memoized: fib(50) returns instantly. But a teammate asks: 'Is recursion itself the problem?'
options: Yes — recursion is dangerous
'No — the problem was repeated work, not recursion. Memoized recursion is O(n) time and O(n) space; iterative is O(n) time and O(1) space. Pick by the trade-off, not by fear.'
Rewrite everything iteratively to be safe
Limit recursion depth globally
steps.explain: Blaming recursion misses the lesson: the enemy was exponential repeated work. Compare the actual trade-offs (time vs. space, clarity vs. constants) instead of banning the technique. Complexity analysis, not superstition.

steps.symptom: Fixed and fast. What do you add to code review so the next exponential does not ship?
evidence: Team: 'How do we catch these in review?'
options: Ban recursion in review guidelines
Add a review checklist item: for any recursive or nested-loop code, state the complexity in Big-O in the PR description — and test at 10x the expected input size
Require benchmarks for every PR
Trust senior reviewers to spot it
steps.explain: Make complexity explicit and testable: Big-O in the PR description forces the author to think, and 10x input tests turn 'works on my data' into 'works at scale.' Exponentials hide at small n — test at large n.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed the complexity class, not the code; defended recursion with trade-offs; and made Big-O explicit in review. Performance bugs are complexity bugs wearing a trench coat.

simulations.title: Two generals, one deploy
simulations.brief: Two data centers must switch traffic at the same instant — but the link between them can drop any message. The plan requires perfect coordination. Decide what is actually achievable.

steps.symptom: The cutover plan: DC-A and DC-B flip simultaneously at midnight, confirmed by message. The link drops ~1% of messages.
evidence:
DC-A and DC-B flip at 00:00, coordinated by messages
Link: 1% message loss | requirement: 'perfectly simultaneous'
options: Add retries — with enough retries it will be simultaneous
Recognize the Two Generals impossibility: no finite message exchange guarantees common knowledge over a lossy link — design for the impossibility instead of against it
Use a longer timeout
Get a better link
steps.explain: The Two Generals problem proves perfect coordination over unreliable messaging is impossible — the last acknowledgment is always uncertain. More retries shrink the doubt; they never eliminate it. Impossibility results are design constraints, not problems to out-stubborn.

steps.symptom: Perfect simultaneity is impossible. The business still needs a cutover Friday.
evidence:
Cutover: Friday | simultaneity: impossible
Need: safe, not perfect
options: Cancel the cutover
Design around it: make the flip idempotent and time-bounded — either DC can flip safely alone, both flip within a window, and the system converges instead of coordinating
Flip both and hope the messages arrive
Flip one, wait an hour, flip the other
steps.explain: When coordination is impossible, design systems that do not need it: idempotent flips, convergence windows, and either-side-safe operations. The great distributed-systems trick is replacing 'agree then act' with 'act safely without agreeing.'

steps.symptom: Cutover succeeded via convergence. An architect asks: 'So when CAN two systems agree?'
options: 'Never — give up on distributed systems.'

'With majorities and retries: consensus protocols (Paxos/Raft-style) give practical agreement with high probability under partial synchrony — not perfect certainty, but engineered reliability. Theory sets the ceiling; protocols work the room below it.'
'With a perfect network.'
'With blockchain.'
steps.explain: Impossibility of perfection does not mean impossibility of practice: consensus protocols deliver agreement that is reliable enough to bet businesses on, under stated assumptions. The honest answer names both the ceiling and the room.

simulations.debrief: You accepted the impossibility, designed for convergence instead of coordination, and explained the practical middle. Theory's 'impossible' is the beginning of engineering, not the end.

simulations.title: The regex that ate the server
simulations.brief: A user submitted a 40-character string and the validation regex has been running for six minutes at 100% CPU. It is catastrophic backtracking. Respond.

steps.symptom: One 40-character input, one regex, six minutes of 100% CPU. The pattern: ^(a+)+$ against 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaab'.
evidence:
Pattern: ^(a+)+$ | input: 31 a's + 'b'
CPU: 100% for 6+ min | service: validation endpoint
options: Kill the process and move on
Kill it, then understand: nested quantifiers create exponential backtracking paths — the engine tries every way to split the a's before failing. This is ReDoS, and the fix is structural
Add more CPU so it finishes faster
Ban the user who submitted the string
steps.explain: Catastrophic backtracking is exponential: (a+)+ against a non-matching string explores ~2^n partitions. Killing the process stops the bleeding; understanding the mechanism prevents the recurrence. The input was not an attack — it was a fuzzer doing you a favor.

steps.symptom: Understood. Now fix the validation so this class of incident dies.
evidence: Kill the ReDoS class, not just this regex
options: Rewrite this one regex more carefully
Defense in depth: rewrite without nested quantifiers (^a+$), add a regex timeout to the engine, and cap input length before matching — one fix is a patch, three is a posture
Remove regex validation entirely
Only allow alphanumeric input everywhere
steps.explain: One careful regex is one careful regex — the next author writes the next bomb. Structural defenses (no nested quantifiers as a lint rule, engine timeouts, input caps) protect against the whole class. Fix the instance AND the category.

steps.symptom: Fixed. A teammate asks: 'How do I know if MY regex is dangerous?'
options: 'Regexes are fine, don't worry.'
'Nested quantifiers (a+)+, (a*)*, (a|b+)+ are the smell — and test every regex against a long near-miss input. If it does not return instantly, it is exponential.'
'Avoid regex entirely.'
'Only use regexes from Stack Overflow.'
steps.explain: Teach the smell and the test: nested quantifiers are the warning sign, and the near-miss stress test (long input that almost matches) is the detector. Theory made visible: exponential blowup you can feel in your terminal.

simulations.debrief: You killed the process, learned the mechanism, defended the whole class, and taught the smell. A 40-character string taught the team more about complexity than a semester of lectures.

consoleSims.title: Breakpoint the loop
consoleSims.brief: You are studying how total() accumulates. Open app.py and set a breakpoint on line 3 — the loop header — to watch each iteration.

tasks.instruction: Set a breakpoint on line 3 of app.py.
tasks.hint: Toggle a breakpoint: FILE=app.py, LINE=3 (the loop header).

consoleSims.debrief: Breakpoints on loop headers let you watch iteration happen. Observing execution is how abstract complexity becomes concrete.

consoleSims.title: Retarget the service port
consoleSims.brief: The deployment spec moved the service to port 9090. Open config.yaml and change line 2 to set the port — precision matters in configuration.

tasks.instruction: Fix line 2 of config.yaml to read exactly: two spaces, then 'port: 9090'.
tasks.hint: Fix line 2: FILE=config.yaml, LINE=2, TEXT='  port: 9090' (keep the two-space indent).

consoleSims.debrief: Configuration is code: exact, reviewed, and precise. One wrong character and the theory meets reality.

consoleSims.title: Query the truth table
consoleSims.brief: Relational logic is logic made executable. Run a SELECT query — the console validates that your SQL actually selects.

tasks.instruction: Run a SQL query beginning with SELECT.
tasks.hint: Type a query containing SELECT, e.g. SELECT * FROM measurements.

consoleSims.debrief: SELECT is existential quantification with a WHERE clause. Logic, but it returns rows.

consoleSims.title: File the complexity worksheet
consoleSims.brief: Every algorithm you study gets a worksheet: its complexity class and your contact. Set the fields and submit — written analysis beats remembered analysis.

tasks.instruction: Set the site_name field to 'Complexity worksheet'.

consoleSims.debrief: Write the complexity down. An analysis that lives only in your head cannot be checked.

terminalMissions.title: Who is reasoning
terminalMissions.brief: Arguments have authors. Print your username.

terminalMissions.title: List the axioms
terminalMissions.brief: Every proof starts from givens. List what is available here.
terminalMissions.success_message: Givens listed. State your axioms before your theorems.

terminalMissions.title: State the complexity class
terminalMissions.brief: A loop with a constant bound is constant time. State the class with echo: O(1).

checks.hint: Run: echo O(1) — name the class.

terminalMissions.success_message: O(1) stated. Name the class; do not just feel it.

terminalMissions.title: Name the machine
terminalMissions.brief: Computation happens on machines. Print the hostname.
terminalMissions.success_message: Machine named. Abstract machines still run somewhere.

terminalMissions.title: Locate the observer
terminalMissions.brief: Print your working directory — the observer has a position.
terminalMissions.success_message: Observer located. Even pure reason runs from somewhere.

terminalMissions.title: Sign the proof
terminalMissions.brief: Conclude with QED via echo, then print your identity record — the prover signs the proof.
terminalMissions.success_message: QED, signed. Verify, do not trust.

terminalMissions.title: Identify the platform
terminalMissions.brief: Print the full platform string, then your username — the proof records its machine and its author.
terminalMissions.success_message: Platform and author recorded. Reproducibility is a virtue, even in theory.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
